standard.title: Significant individuals in Medieval Europe
standard.description: the role and achievements of a significant individual and/or group in Medieval, Renaissance or pre-modern Europe
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explain the role and achievements of a significant individual in an ancient society (AC9HH7K13). They understand how to investigate an individual's significance using evidence. They have not yet applied this to a medieval or early modern European context — including the institutional role of the Catholic Church, Renaissance figures, or individuals who shaped political and religious reform.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the role and achievements of a significant individual or group in Medieval, Renaissance or pre-modern Europe — describing what they did, why it mattered in their historical context, and what legacy their achievements left for later developments.

nodes.label: Establishing historical significance
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what makes an individual or group historically significant — using criteria such as influence, scale of impact and legacy — and apply these criteria to identify the chosen subject as significant.
nodes.minimum_width: Application of at least two criteria of significance to the chosen individual or group.
nodes.typical_width: Multiple criteria of significance (influence on contemporaries, scale of impact, legacy for later periods) applied to the chosen subject; initial identification of what the individual or group achieved and why it mattered.
wider: Compare the significance of two candidates (e.g. Galileo vs Martin Luther) using the same criteria to develop a defensible judgement about which was more historically significant
Examine how historical significance is constructed — why some individuals are remembered and others forgotten — using the Church's influence in determining which figures were celebrated or condemned
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a working understanding of historical significance as a concept with criteria, students cannot distinguish between an individual being interesting and being historically significant. All subsequent analysis of role and achievement depends on this frame.

response_modes.reason: Students often assume that famous = significant. Scaffold the reasoning explicitly: significance is about influence, scale, duration and legacy — not celebrity. Apply the criteria to the chosen subject step by step.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two criteria of historical significance and applies them to the chosen individual or group
Explains why the chosen subject qualifies as historically significant rather than merely notable

nodes.label: Role in historical context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the role of the chosen individual or group in their specific historical context — including the conditions that enabled their influence — drawing on primary and secondary sources as evidence.
nodes.minimum_width: A description of the chosen individual or group's role with at least one source as evidence.
nodes.typical_width: A well-contextualised account of the role — including the social, political or religious conditions that enabled it — using multiple sources; the role of the Catholic Church in provision of social services, education and feudal organisation; or the influence of Renaissance patrons such as the Medici family; or political figures such as Henry VIII, Elizabeth I, Martin Luther or Louis XIV.
wider: Use visual sources such as the illustration of Hell in the Hortus Deliciarum (Herrad of Landsberg) to examine the Church's role in shaping beliefs and social control
Examine Lucrezia Borgia as a case study in how gender, political alliance and historiography intersect in assessing a significant individual's role

response_modes.reason: The range of possible subjects for this standard is very wide — Church, Medici, scientific figures, political reformers. Varying the type of source used (visual, written, architectural) helps students see that historical role can be evidenced in multiple ways.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Medici family as bankers, merchants and arts patrons — alongside the Catholic Church as institutional actor — offers a rich contrast between individual and group significance that deepens students' understanding of how influence operates in medieval society.
success_criteria: Describes the role of the chosen individual or group using at least one primary or secondary source as evidence
Explains at least one condition (social, political, religious or economic) that enabled the individual or group to exercise influence

nodes.label: Achievements and their impact
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the achievements of the chosen individual or group and describe their impact on contemporaries and on later developments.
nodes.minimum_width: At least two achievements of the chosen individual or group with an explanation of their impact.
nodes.typical_width: Multiple achievements analysed for both immediate and longer-term impact; the Scientific Revolution as a case study in how individual discoveries (Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler, Newton) collectively overturned traditional views and contributed to science as an alternative to Church authority; Oliver Cromwell's role in the English Civil War and parliamentary development.
wider: Examine the importance of the Scientific Revolution — particularly how Copernicus, Galileo and Newton's theories overturned traditional views of planetary motion — and how this contributed to science being seen as an alternative to the Church as a source of truth

Investigate how the significance of Oliver Cromwell and the execution of Charles I contributed to the development of the Westminster parliamentary system, tracing achievement through to modern institutions

response_modes.reason: Students often list achievements without connecting them to impact. Scaffold the logic: achievement X had impact Y on contemporaries, and its longer-term legacy was Z. Each achievement needs an explicitly reasoned chain of consequence.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two achievements of the chosen individual or group
Explains the impact of at least one achievement on contemporaries and on later historical developments

nodes.label: Legacy and historical judgement
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the legacy of the chosen individual or group — explaining what endured from their achievements and how historians have judged their significance — and connect this legacy to the development of the modern world.
nodes.minimum_width: An explanation of at least one lasting legacy of the chosen individual or group and a connection to a feature of the modern world.
nodes.typical_width: Legacy assessed through multiple criteria; how historians' judgements of significance have changed over time; the enduring impact of the Catholic Church, the Medici, key Enlightenment figures or scientific revolutionaries on modern political, religious or intellectual life.
wider: Examine how the influences and contributions of individuals such as Machiavelli, Luther or Louis XIV have been reinterpreted across different historical periods, showing that legacy is not fixed

Investigate why the achievements of women such as Lucrezia Borgia or Elizabeth I have historically been undervalued or misrepresented, connecting this to historiographical questions about who is deemed significant

response_modes.reason: Legacy assessment integrates significance criteria (Node 1), contextual role (Node 2) and impact analysis (Node 3). Invest in helping students articulate a coherent historical judgement that draws on all three rather than treating legacy as a separate summary.

success_criteria: Explains at least one lasting legacy of the chosen individual or group and connects it to a feature of the modern world
Evaluates the significance of the individual or group using evidence, not just assertion
